episodes.title: Why Treasuries Are 'Risky' Again
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Odd Lots hosts Carolyn Fluger, an economist studying how monetary policy reaction functions and treasury bond risk have evolved, against a backdrop of a surging US 30-year yield (5.592%, highest since 2002) even after a recent Fed rate cut. The discussion centers on why treasuries have become riskier (more stock-correlated) over the past five years and what that means for yields, inflation credibility, and US financial hegemony — all directly relevant to a global rates desk pricing US duration and the dollar's safe-haven status.

**Key points**
- US 30-year yield at 5.592%, highest since 2002, rising sharply despite a recent Fed rate hike/cut (hosts note confusion over direction), raising questions about whether policy is dampening financial conditions.
- Fluger's research (with Bauer and Sundaram) shows the Fed's perceived policy reaction function was nearly flat in 2020-21 (rates expected near zero despite 5-6% inflation surprises) and only steepened after the Fed actually began hiking in 2022 — a "learning from actions" channel.
- Treasury-stock correlation has flipped positive again recently (bonds act "risky"/stock-like), reversing the post-2000 negative-correlation regime; a large share of the 2020-2025 yield rise is attributed to this rising bond riskiness rather than inflation expectations, which have stayed stable.
- Chinese 30-year bond yield cited at ~2% vs US 30yr ~5.6%, a 300-350bp spread that has blown out since late 2020/2018-19 (coinciding with China's bond index inclusion) — framed as a possible marker of shifting financial hegemony.

**FX / rates implications**
- Rising UST term premium and risky-bond dynamics support continued upward pressure on US long-end yields and a firmer-for-longer USD/DXY backdrop, a headwind for EM carry trades (INR, IDR, MXN, BRL rates) via the global risk-free rate channel.
- Persistent US fiscal deficits, AI-capex-driven borrowing, and debated Fed credibility could keep term premia elevated, implying EM central banks may need to maintain wider rate buffers over UST to defend currencies and attract flows.
- Widening UST-China yield spread signals diverging growth/policy trajectories; not directly actionable for EM but relevant context for global capital flow narratives.

**Watch list**
- Further moves in the 30-year UST yield and any Fed communication on its reaction function/credibility framework.
- Supply-driven narratives (deficits, AI hyperscaler borrowing) versus risk-premium repricing as the dominant driver of long-end yields.

episodes.title: Cut to the Chase! Policy credibility concerns
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Standard Chartered's Steve Price examines the global march higher in long-dated government bond yields through the first nine months of the year, arguing it reflects fading policy credibility on both fiscal and monetary fronts rather than just energy-driven inflation — a theme with direct implications for global risk appetite and EM carry trades.

**Key points**
- Year-to-date 10-year yield moves: US +114bps, UK +93bps, France +115bps, Germany +62bps, Japan +97bps.
- Initial catalyst was Middle East conflict pushing oil prices higher, fueling short-term inflation fears and central bank hawkishness.
- Despite recent softer US inflation and employment data, falling oil prices, and Fed members signaling a hike at the October 28 meeting is unlikely, US 10-year yields remain higher than a week ago — seen as a credibility warning sign.
- Rising debt-servicing costs as a share of GDP are both a cause and effect of higher yields; Europe faces limited fiscal room given already-high tax rates plus looming AI infrastructure and defense spending needs; the US has no visible political path to address its budget deficit.
- The Fed is caught between presidential pressure for lower rates (to ease borrowing costs) and a resilient economy with still-elevated inflation arguing for stable-to-higher rates.

**FX / rates implications**
- Fading fiscal/monetary credibility in DM sovereigns keeps term premia elevated, a headwind for duration broadly and a factor EM rates desks should track given co-movement with UST yields.
- Standard Chartered's house view: expect continued volatility over the near term but believes yields look increasingly attractive on a 6-12 month horizon and equities should grind higher — framing any downside (yield spike/equity selloff) as a buying opportunity, which supports a constructive medium-term backdrop for EM carry and risk assets.
- Fed policy path uncertainty (political pressure vs. inflation/growth resilience) is a key swing factor for USD and EM FX funding costs.

**Watch list**
- Next FOMC meeting October 28 — markets currently pricing a hike as unlikely.
- Further UST, Gilt, Bund, and JGB yield moves as a gauge of sovereign credibility concerns.
- Oil price trajectory tied to Middle East conflict developments.

episodes.title: Inside Norway's sovereign wealth fund dilemma to divest from Israel
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Norway's $2.3 trillion sovereign wealth fund — the world's largest, funded by oil and gas revenue — is navigating a politically charged ethics crisis over its Israel-linked holdings, highlighting how geopolitics increasingly intrudes on even the most passive global capital allocators.

**Key points**
- The fund holds stakes in roughly 7,000 companies, including nearly every major global stock (Nvidia, Apple, Amazon, Google, JPMorgan), and funds almost 20% of Norway's annual government budget.
- It is overwhelmingly passive, tracking broad market indices, but an independent ethics committee bars investment in select firms (tobacco, coal, nuclear weapons, defense contractors like Boeing and Lockheed Martin).
- In August, the fund divested from some Israeli stocks and from Caterpillar, after Israel used Caterpillar bulldozers in Gaza — triggering domestic political backlash and US criticism (White House, late Senator Lindsey Graham) over perceived foreign-policy overreach.
- In November, Norway's parliament suspended part of the ethics guidelines to avoid forcing divestment from big tech (Microsoft, Amazon, Alphabet) tied to Israeli defense/government contracts; a government review report is due shortly.

**FX / rates implications**
- Minimal direct read-through for EM FX/rates; this is a governance/equity-allocation story, not a monetary-policy or flows catalyst affecting NOK, USD, or EM currencies.
- Relevant mainly as a case study in how geopolitical risk (Israel-Gaza) can intersect with large sovereign capital pools' equity allocation decisions, a theme that recurs across other sovereign wealth funds (Gulf states) relevant to global risk sentiment.

**Watch list**
- Norway's government ethics-guideline review report, due imminently, which could reshape how the fund screens future holdings (Caterpillar, big tech, defense names).
- Any follow-on US political/trade retaliation rhetoric tied to foreign sovereign funds divesting from US companies.

episodes.title: In Focus: Critical Chemicals
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
JP Morgan's industry/policy thematics team examines critical chemicals as an under-the-radar but foundational US-China economic security vulnerability, paralleling the critical minerals/rare earths dynamic that has already roiled markets. For an EM trader, this is a structural read on US-China strategic competition and the policy trajectory toward export controls, taxonomies and critical-materials lists — the same playbook that previously triggered rare earth export restrictions and market volatility in 2025.

**Key points**
- China controls roughly 35% of global chemical output (compressing to 28%/24% on value-added basis) and 41% of chemical innovation ('chemical space') versus just 11% for the US.
- China controls raw/key starting materials for 94% of amoxicillin production; Europe imports ~70% of cotton linters (defense/ammunition input) from China.
- Semiconductors require ~500 chemical processes; a single missing molecule can halt production lines despite low direct cost — echoing the 2021 auto chip shortage.
- Chemical investment is ~75-80% M&A/consolidation, with little venture capital, private equity or greenfield investment — a warning sign versus innovation-building activity.
- Proposed US policy response: a critical chemicals taxonomy to map supply-chain dependencies, plus a US critical chemicals list (modeled on the 2018 critical minerals list) to galvanize action.

**FX / rates implications**
- Reinforces the broader US-China strategic decoupling theme already pressuring CNY/CNH sentiment and feeding into tariff/export-control risk that spills into regional Asia FX (KRW, TWD, MYR) via supply-chain linkages.
- Signals continued US/allied policy momentum toward critical-materials export controls and lists — a template that previously triggered China rare-earth restrictions in 2025, a risk-off catalyst for Asia FX and a driver of USD safe-haven demand.
- Longer-term industrial policy push (reshoring, allied coordination) supports a structurally firm USD/onshoring narrative with mixed implications for EM Asia manufacturing-linked currencies.

**Watch list**
- Any formal announcement of a US critical chemicals list or taxonomy, which could presage targeted export controls or tariff actions on Chinese chemical inputs.
- Further Chinese export-control actions on chemicals/rare earths following the precedent set in 2025, a potential volatility trigger for CNY and regional Asia FX.
- Xi-US White House engagement follow-through on broader trade/competition dynamics referenced in the episode.

episodes.title: Credit Crunch: Investor Survey 4Q - Rate Bears Hoard Rally Cash
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Bloomberg Intelligence's 4Q Credit Investor Survey shows high-yield investors turning sharply bearish, piling into cash, and flipping net underweight on rates for the first time in several quarters, even as spreads have cheapened meaningfully. The discussion centers on US/European credit and rates but carries broader risk-sentiment signals relevant to global macro positioning.

**Key points**
- High-yield returns are flat-to-negative YTD after a weak September/October sell-off; survey respondents expect a net 34% loss for 4Q (up from 15% in 3Q).
- Spreads have widened ~75bp (260 to 335 OAS), now about 1.43-1.6 standard deviations cheap versus history, yet the survey's rich/fair/cheap net reading was 44% "rich" — seen as contrarian bullish.
- Average cash holdings rose to 5.5%, near all-time highs, signaling dry powder for a rally once rates roll over.
- Rates/yields cited as the number-one market driver, ahead of geopolitics (Iran war), earnings, and EU recession (seen as unlikely); money markets pricing ~4 Fed-equivalent hikes, guest sees 2 as more likely.
- Default forecasts (2.3%) remain far above realized defaults (0.5%, two defaults all year), continuing a persistent survey over-bearishness pattern.
- 4Q supply forecast at 15bn (index-eligible), below reality seen in prior quarters; US still preferred over Europe in local-currency terms (net 20%), though the guest favors Europe on rate-rollover and dispersion potential.
- France's OAT-Bund spread near 122.5bp flagged as a drag on European high yield given France's large weight in EU credit indices.

**FX / rates implications**
- A continued "bear flattening" of the US curve and uncertain Fed path (2-4 hikes priced) is the key global read-through: further UST repricing would keep DXY firm and pressure EM carry trades broadly.
- Oil price trajectory (tied to the ongoing war) feeding into core inflation is flagged as a swing factor for how much further the Fed/ECB tightening cycle extends — relevant for EM central banks' own hike/cut calculus.
- Record-high cash balances among global credit investors suggest significant sidelines liquidity that could rotate into risk assets (including EM credit/FX) once rate volatility peaks.

**Watch list**
- US midterm elections in November — outcome could reshape trade-tariff policy and geopolitical risk pricing.
- Trajectory of oil prices and the Iran-related conflict as inputs to core inflation and central bank paths.
- Whether credit spreads cross the 2-standard-deviation cheap threshold, flagged as the technical trigger for a potential turn/rally in risk assets.

episodes.title: Week That Was - 2 Oct: Indian Markets Slip as Global Yields Stay Near Two-Decade Highs
episodes.summary:
**Summary**
Indian markets sold off over the week as global bond yields stayed near two-decade highs, pressuring the rupee and local bonds even as India's domestic macro data remained encouraging. The sell-off was primarily a global transmission story via yields rather than domestic fundamentals, with focus now shifting to RBI's MPC meeting.

**Key points**
- Nifty fell about 3.1% and Sensex 2.7% on the week; broad-based sectoral declines led by Auto (-6%), FMCG (-4.7%), Metals (-4.1%); IT was the lone gainer, helped by easing dollar/Fed hike concerns.
- Rupee weakened ~0.5% to trade near 96.3/USD as elevated global yields pressured EM currencies broadly.
- India 10-year G-Sec yield rose ~9bps to 7.21%, highest in over two years; 5-year up ~12bps, 3-year up ~4bps, tracking UST 10y which rose ~11bps on the week.
- India macro remained solid: manufacturing PMI hit a 7-month high of 55.1 (from 52.8), GST collections up 14.7% y/y, IIP up ~8% y/y in August; trade deficit narrowed to ~$27bn from ~$32bn.
- Fiscal deficit (Apr-Aug) at ~42% of full-year budget estimate, slightly above last year's pace.
- US jobs data soft (29k added, unemployment at 4.2%, August revised down to 13k); US-China agreed limited tariff relief on ~$30bn of trade each way.
- Oil eased ~2% to ~$102/bbl on G7's 100m-barrel strategic reserve release and Middle East export flows normalizing; gold fell 2.4% in rupee terms on elevated yields.

**FX / rates implications**
- USDINR drifting toward 96.3 reflects broad EM FX pressure from elevated UST yields; watch for further rupee weakness if global yields stay near 2-decade highs.
- Markets increasingly pricing a hawkish RBI tilt at the MPC meeting given inflation/import-bill concerns from higher oil-linked costs and currency pressure — a hawkish surprise would support INR but pressure front-end rates further.
- India's bond supply concerns are compounding the global yield pressure, keeping the 10-year GSec near multi-year highs; the rupee-bond-yield linkage is the key transmission channel to watch rather than domestic growth.

**Watch list**
- RBI MPC decision on October 7 — key test of hawkish repricing.
- Q2 earnings season kicking off this week — could offset or compound rate-driven equity weakness.
- US Treasury yield trajectory — continued elevation near two-decade highs remains the primary external driver for INR and GSec yields.
